pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Dissolving & Solutions

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 Properties & changes of materials):** Pupils should be taught to know that some materials will dissolve in liquid to form a solution, and describe how to recover a substance from a solution.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-2 / 5-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-2] (e.g. dissolving), the total weight of matter is conserved; develop a model [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1].

- **Operational details:** The load-bearing idea is CONSERVATION: when a soluble solid dissolves it does NOT disappear — it breaks into pieces far too small to see and spreads evenly through the liquid to form a clear solution, and it can be RECOVERED by evaporating the liquid. Teach with the whole-system move: mass the sealed jar of water + sugar BEFORE and AFTER dissolving — the reading is unchanged, proving the sugar is still there. Then evaporate a little salt solution to reveal the solid returning. Distinguish dissolve from melt, and soluble from insoluble (sand does not dissolve — it can be filtered). Introduce saturation lightly (a limit to how much dissolves). Keep the explanation at 'tiny pieces too small to see' — formal particle theory is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal, quantitative). The child predicts and confirms that mass is conserved when a solid dissolves, explains that the dissolved solid is still present, and describes evaporation as the way to recover it.
bestPractices: Use the whole-system mass check: weigh water + solid before and after dissolving so the unchanged reading proves the solid is still present.
Recover the solid by evaporation so the child sees dissolving is reversible and the matter was never lost.
Contrast soluble vs insoluble with a control (sand) that is separated by filtering, not dissolving.
Explain dissolving as the solid breaking into pieces too small to see and spreading evenly, without invoking formal particle theory (KS3).
Introduce saturation lightly with a 'keep adding until it stops dissolving' path.
keyRepresentations: A dissolve tank on a balance showing an unchanged reading before/after
A zoom-in showing the solid splitting into too-small-to-see bits spreading through the liquid
An evaporate step recovering the crystals
An insoluble control (sand) filtered out, and a saturation limit
commonMisconceptions: A dissolved solid has disappeared or been destroyed (Piagetian intuition).
Dissolving and melting are the same process.
The mass of the solution is less than water + solid because 'the sugar is gone'.
Anything can dissolve if you stir enough (missing insolubility and saturation).
The solid cannot be got back once dissolved (missing recovery by evaporation).

learn.summary: Teach conservation of mass during dissolving for ages 9–10: a soluble solid that dissolves does not disappear but breaks into pieces too small to see and spreads evenly through the liquid to form a clear solution, and can be recovered by evaporation. The load-bearing move is weighing the whole system (water + solid) in a sealed/covered container and comparing the reading before and after the solid dissolves to show it is unchanged, then evaporating a solution to recover the solid. Distinguish dissolving from melting, soluble from insoluble (sand can be filtered), and introduce saturation lightly. Keep the explanation at 'tiny pieces too small to see'; formal particle theory is later (KS3).

activities.title: Dissolve, weigh, recover bench
feedback: If a learner predicts the reading will drop as the sugar dissolves, draw attention to the unchanged balance in the sealed jar: the weight did not leave, so the solid cannot have disappeared.

If a learner says the solid is 'gone' or 'turned into water', run the evaporation step together so the solid reappears — show, don't just assert. (Use the salt solution for heated evaporation. Heating a sugar solution strongly tends to make syrup or caramel, so to get sugar crystals back, leave the solution to evaporate slowly at room temperature.)
If a learner expects sand to dissolve like sugar, contrast the two: sand stays visible and is filtered out, showing dissolving depends on the substances.
When extra sugar stops dissolving and settles, name this as saturation — a limit to how much the liquid can hold.
Keep the container covered or sealed: the conservation claim is that the reading is the same before and after dissolving, which an open jar can confound by losing water to evaporation over time.
activities.rationale: The curriculum asks children to support conservation with measurement (NGSS 5-PS1-2 measures quantities to evidence that total weight is conserved); a measured, observed before/after reading on a sealed whole system plus recovery by evaporation can target the intuition that dissolving destroys matter. Recording the reading with the solid present but undissolved, then again once dissolved, isolates the conservation point rather than merely showing that adding solid raises the reading. Contrasting a soluble solid with an insoluble control and a saturation limit builds the distinctions the standards require.

NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph quantities to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change (incl dissolving); 5-PS1-1 matter is particles too small to see
Children hold a Piagetian 'the sugar disappears/is destroyed' view; measuring mass before and after and evaporating to recover the solid targets it; 'think about the whole system'
learnerActions: Place a jar of water on a balance, add a measured spoon of sugar, and cover or seal the jar so no matter can escape or enter during the experiment.
Record this starting reading while the sugar is still visible and has not yet dissolved.
Predict whether the reading will go up, down, or stay the same as the sugar dissolves, and state WHY, before stirring.
Stir and watch the grains break into finer and finer specks that spread out until the water looks clear.

Read the balance again and compare with the starting reading: in a sealed jar it should be the same, apart from tiny flickers within the balance's precision. The dissolved sugar's weight is still there, so the sugar cannot have disappeared.
Place a shallow salt solution under a heat/evaporation step, let the water steam away, and watch the salt crystals reappear.
Try a sand control: stir it in and observe that it stays visible and settles, then separate it by filtering rather than dissolving.
Follow a 'keep adding sugar' path until extra sugar settles undissolved, to meet a saturation limit.
activities.intendedInsight: When a soluble solid dissolves it is still present — spread through the liquid as bits too small to see — because the sealed system weighs the same before and after it dissolves; and it can be recovered by evaporating the liquid. Some solids (sand) do not dissolve in water and can be filtered, and there is a limit to how much will dissolve (saturation).

activities.title: Zoom-in: where did the sugar go?
feedback: If a learner says the clear liquid is 'just water', revisit the zoom-in showing the bits spread throughout, and the recovery step that returns the solid.
Reinforce the vocabulary: solid + liquid → solution; evaporation returns the solid.
activities.rationale: A revealable diagram communicates the dissolving-and-recovery sequence and vocabulary and the 'still here' idea, serving as a companion to measured work. It makes the invisible dispersion visible, but on its own it asserts rather than demonstrates conservation, so it supports rather than replaces the weigh-it-yourself experience.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: some materials dissolve in liquid to form a solution; pupils describe how to recover a substance from a solution
learnerActions: Reveal a magnified view of a dissolving grain splitting into ever-smaller specks that spread through the liquid.
Trace the sequence dissolving → solution → evaporate → recovered solid, lifting a 'the sugar is still here' flap at the solution stage.
State in your own words why the clear solution still contains the solid.
activities.intendedInsight: A dissolved solid becomes clear not because it vanished but because it has broken into pieces too small to see and spread evenly; the sequence can be reversed to recover the solid.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain and check your reasoning
feedback: A prediction that the reading will fall as the salt dissolves signals the 'dissolving destroys matter' misconception; use evaporation and the before/after balance to show mass is conserved.

If a learner explains the vanishing as melting, clarify the distinction: dissolving is a solid mixing into a liquid (a second substance is needed), while melting is one substance turning from solid to liquid when it is heated; then rebuild the conservation idea.
If a learner predicts sand or flour will dissolve like salt, contrast soluble and insoluble and note the saturation limit — dissolving depends on the substances and there is a limit.
Keep the two weight claims distinct: 'heavier than plain water' comes from adding the salt, whereas 'unchanged just before versus just after dissolving' is what shows the matter was conserved.
'Still there' with no way to check is memorised, not understood: push for at least one recovery or test method.
activities.rationale: The 'how do you know' tier separates a child who holds matter conservation (offers taste/weigh/evaporate) from one who thinks dissolving destroys the solid. Requiring prediction-with-reason before observation surfaces the diagnostic reasoning; requiring a recovery method guards against rote recall. A predict-and-question format like this can be used while teaching, not only to assess; on its own, recognition responses do not elicit independent construction of the conservation argument.

learnerActions: Weigh a glass of plain water and record the reading. Add a spoon of salt without stirring, cover the glass if possible, and record the reading again while the salt is still visible. Before stirring, predict whether the balance will read more, less, or the same as this second reading once the salt has dissolved, and say why.
Stir until the salt is invisible, read the balance, and compare it with both earlier readings (plain water, and water with undissolved salt) and with your prediction.

Note the two distinct comparisons: the salty water weighs MORE than the plain water you started with (because you added salt), while the reading is UNCHANGED from just before to just after the salt dissolves (the conservation point).

Answer probing questions: If all the water dried up, what would be left, and does that show the salt was there all along? Would salty water weigh more, less, or the same as the plain water you started with, and why? If it had been sand instead of salt, would stirring make it disappear — what's different? Is salty water one substance or a mixture of two, and how would you argue it?

Give the most important part: how you KNOW the salt is still there — weight, evaporating it to find it left behind, or taste (only if the teacher says so, using clean food-safe cups, never science equipment).
activities.intendedInsight: A full understanding says the solid is still there AND offers converging evidence — weight, taste, and recoverability by evaporation — not just a memorised 'still there'. It also transfers: sand won't dissolve, and solutions can saturate.

constraints: Keep the explanation at 'pieces too small to see' spreading evenly; do not introduce formal particle theory, which belongs to later study (KS3).

A revealable diagram or flap communicates sequence and vocabulary but cannot let the learner watch the balance hold steady or drive recovery; use it as a companion, not a substitute, for measured work.

A fixed quiz (slider for 'what will the balance read?', MCQs on soluble/insoluble and recovery) can check understanding but does not provide the weigh-it-yourself experience; recognition responses do not elicit independent construction of the conservation argument.

Weigh the whole system in a sealed/covered container so evaporation during the experiment does not confound the before/after mass comparison; record the reading with the solid present but undissolved, then again once dissolved.
Distinguish the represented idea from the setup: evaporation recovers the solid but requires appropriate heat safety for a classroom evaporating-dish activity.

Insolubility and saturation outcomes depend on the specific materials and amounts used; frame sand as a chosen insoluble control and 'extra sugar settles' as the observed saturation limit for that setup, not a universal rule for all solids.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The ACS Inquiry in Action source supporting the Piagetian misconception and whole-system framing is marked unverified in the source row; treat the misconception-targeting and 'whole system' claims as legacy, not independently confirmed here.

The source POE describes weighing an open glass of water and adding salt, with the glass+water+salt expected to read 'heavier by the salt's weight'. Over a longer dissolving period an open container can lose mass to evaporation; prefer a sealed/covered system for the strict conservation demonstration, and keep 'heavier than plain water' (true: you added salt) distinct from 'unchanged before vs after dissolving' (the conservation point). Both framings appear in the source and are kept distinct.

The preferred bench takes the starting reading with the solid present but undissolved (whole-system move), rather than a water-only baseline followed by adding solid, which would show mass addition instead of conservation during dissolving.

The activity-1 rationale was softened from the original 'conservation is a claim the child must weigh to believe / impossible in static media' to a scoped, curriculum-grounded statement; comparative necessity of the measured medium is not established by the available sources.

Claims in the original that conservation is 'impossible in static media', that 3D 'adds nothing', and that discussion/chat 'cannot teach' conservation have been softened to scoped affordances and objective limits.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: weigh a glass of water on a balance, note the reading, then ask the child to predict what the balance shows AFTER a spoon of salt is stirred in until invisible — and crucially WHY. A child who thinks dissolving destroys matter predicts the same or a lower reading. Stir, watch it vanish, read the balance (heavier by the salt's weight). The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I let all the water dry up, what would I find in the glass — and does that tell you the salt was there all along?
Would the glass-of-salty-water weigh more, less, or the same as the plain water I started with? Why?
What if it had been sand instead of salt — would stirring make it disappear? What's different?
Is the salty water one substance or a mixture of two? How would you argue it?
assess.correctAnswer: The salt is still there, dissolved — spread through the water as pieces too small to see, making a solution. You know because you could taste it (salty), weigh it (glass+water+salt weighs the same as before, more than plain water), or let the water evaporate and find the salt left behind.

errorPatterns.pattern: the dissolved solid has been destroyed ('it turned into water' / 'it's gone')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaporate the solution together so the salt reappears; weigh before and after to show mass is conserved. This is the Piagetian conservation gap — show, don't just assert.
errorPatterns.distractor: The salt disappeared — it turned into water, so it's gone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: tier one answer 'it's gone' or tier two offering no recovery method

errorPatterns.pattern: dissolving is a kind of melting ('the water melted the salt')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the vocabulary distinction (dissolve needs the liquid; melt needs only heat) before rebuilding the conservation idea.
errorPatterns.distractor: The water melted the salt into liquid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains the vanishing as melting rather than dispersing into the liquid

errorPatterns.pattern: everything dissolves if you stir long enough (no notion of solubility limit or insoluble solids)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast salt (dissolves) with sand (doesn't) and a saturated solution (no more will dissolve) — dissolving depends on the substances, and there is a limit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts sand or flour will dissolve just like salt

responseLevels.gap: Says the salt is gone/destroyed, or 'still there' with no way to check; may call it melting.
responseLevels.full: Salt is still there as a solution; justifies with conservation reasoning (weight unchanged, recoverable by evaporation, still tastable) AND transfers to a new case — predicts sand won't dissolve and a solution can saturate.
responseLevels.partial: Says the salt is still there and names one recovery idea, but treats it as a rote fact — can't connect taste, weight, and evaporation as converging evidence, or over-generalises that everything dissolves.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I stir a spoon of salt into a glass of water and keep stirring until I can't see any salt at all. Is the salt still in the glass or has it gone? Then tell me the most important part: how do you KNOW — what could you do to check?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two 'how do you know' separates a child who believes matter is conserved (offers taste/weigh/evaporate as recovery) from one who thinks dissolving destroys the solid. Both tiers must agree: 'still there' PLUS a recovery method. 'Still there' with no way to check is memorised, not understood.
